# Overview

For your final project, you will design and build an AI solution relevant to your work, research or personal projects, combining **at least two themes** from this course.

You will submit a **1–2 page document** describing your solution and linking to it, and give a **4-minute live presentation** with a demo in class.

# Course Themes

Here is a reminder of the main course themes:

| Week | Theme | Example tools |
|------|-------|---------------|
| W1 [Website/app]{.pill .w1} | Websites and apps | GitHub Pages. Lovable, Replit, etc for more complex apps. |
| W2 [Data]{.pill .w2} | Data analysis and dashboards | ChatGPT Data Analysis, or code through Cursor/VS Code |
| W3 [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} | Customized chatbots | Botpress, internal-facing custom GPTs in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. |
| W4 [Research synthesis]{.pill .w4} | Text analysis and literature synthesis | Iterative text analysis in Google Sheets; literature synthesis and qualitative analysis with NotebookLM. Elicit and SciSpace as alternatives. |
| W5 [Automation]{.pill .w5} | Automations | ChatGPT, Claude scheduled tasks |
| W6 [Visuals]{.pill .w6} | Visual design and video | SVG and image-based designs (ChatGPT, Gemini), Canva, PowerPoint, AI-generated video |

# Project Ideas

The colored tags show which course themes each idea covers. Feel free to adapt any of these or come up with your own.

-   **Paper "digital twin"**: Turn a research paper into a website, perhaps with interactives and simulations. You could then include a graphical abstract, a explainer video, or a chatbot that answers questions about the paper. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} [Visuals]{.pill .w6}

-   **Staff training kit**: You could build a short online mini-course perhaps slides, quizzes, a tutor chatbot, some AI visual aids. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} [Visuals]{.pill .w6}

-   **Model selection study**: Benchmark 3 or 4 models on a task for your organization or personal project, analyze cost, quality and performance. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2}

-   **Tool comparison**: Do one real task in two or three tools (for example, for a data anaylysis task, compare ChatGPT Data Analysis vs. ChatGPT Excel Plugin vs  vs. Codex in VSCode. Or for a literature synthesis task, compare NotebookLM vs. Elicit vs. SciSpace). Measure accuracy and cost, then write up a recommendation report. Share the findings with a website or a video. [Any 2+]{.pill .any}

-   **News monitor**: Build an automation that scans news or policy feeds on a specific topic and structures the information into Google Sheets. Set that sheet to be visible publicly, then use it as the live data source for a website that shows trend charts and a briefing page. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2} [Research synthesis]{.pill .w4} [Automation]{.pill .w5}

-   **Website for your lab or department**: Set up a lab or department website with a Botpress bot trained on its SOPs and FAQs, plus perhaps an intake form that sends automatic triage emails to members of the team. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} [Automation]{.pill .w5}

-   **Job search copilot**: Set up a daily automated scan with ChatGPT that searches job boards for roles that match your profile, extracts them into a Google Sheet, and drafts some notes for each application. Then build an interview-prep chatbot (custom GPT or Botpress) that knows your CV and the saved job ads, and runs mock interviews for each role. [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} [Automation]{.pill .w5}

-   **Data story for a specific audience**: Choose a public dataset and one audience, such as local officials or community members. Use ChatGPT Data Analysis or Cursor to clean and explore the data, then use Gamma to combine the narrative and charts. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2}

-   **Data journalism piece**: Analyze a public dataset and publish an illustrated scrollytelling page with an "ask the data" chatbot. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2} [Chatbot]{.pill .w3} [Visuals]{.pill .w6}

-   **Health campaign**: Use local data to pick a key message on one health issue, then create campaign visuals (flyers, social media graphics), a landing page and a short explainer video. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2} [Visuals]{.pill .w6}

-   **NGO impact showcase**: Turn program data into a clear account of results for potential supporters. [Website/app]{.pill .w1} [Data]{.pill .w2} [Visuals]{.pill .w6}

These are just ideas to get you started, not an exhaustive list. Projects that don't match any of them are very welcome.

# Submission Instructions

## 1. Written document (main submission)

Upload a **1–2 page document** (PDF or Word) to the submission page. It should:

-   **Describe your solution**: the problem or opportunity, who it is for, and what you built.
-   **Link to your solution.** The format depends on your project: it might be a website, a slide deck showing the workflow, a video, or a Google Drive folder with different reports.
-   **Include a table of the tools you used**, with columns for the tool, the course theme it relates to, how you used it, and how you went beyond the standard course content.
-   **Include a section on issues and mitigations**, covering at least two issues.

**The document must be mostly written by you.** We will check it with [Pangram](https://www.pangram.com/){target="_blank"}, an AI-text detector, and it should score **under 50% AI-generated**. Of course, you should use AI to build your solution itself!

### Issues to consider {#issues-to-consider}

For the issues and mitigations section, discuss **at least two** issues that apply to your solution and how you would mitigate them. Some options:

-   **Hallucinations**: Confident-sounding but wrong outputs.
-   **Verifiability**: How hard it is to check whether an output is correct.
-   **Rubber-stamping** ("meat proxy-ism"): A human signs off on AI output they haven't really checked.
-   **AI slop**: Low-effort, generic output, and growing audience fatigue with content that "smells like AI".
-   **Loss of visual and linguistic diversity**: Everything starts to look and sound the same.
-   **Bias toward training data**: Outputs reflect the stereotypes and gaps in the data models were trained on.
-   **Data privacy**: Sensitive data shared with third-party tools.
-   **Prompt injection**: Untrusted input (emails, forms, web pages) giving the AI instructions.
-   **Cost**: Models get expensive at scale.
-   **Lack of reproducibility**: Models are non-deterministic, so the same prompt can give different results.
-   **Lack of explainability**: It is often hard to find out why the model produced a given output.
-   **Skill rot**: Losing skills you no longer practice yourself.
-   **Job displacement**: Effects on the people who used to do this work.

This is a non-exhaustive list. There are many other issues and mitigations that you might consider.

## 2. Live presentation

On the assigned date, you will present your project live in your assigned session (**4 minutes total**). We recommend:

-   Introduction and context (~1 minute)
-   **Live demonstration of your solution** (~2 minutes)
-   Issues, reflections and next steps (~1 minute)

You can present via slides or by simply showing and speaking about your project.

## 3. Share your link

If your project has a URL (for example, a live website, app or chatbot), post it in the comment box on the final project page so classmates and instructors can find it after your presentation.

# Presentation Dates

The final presentations will be on either **Sunday, November 15** or **Wednesday, November 18**. You will be expected to present in your corresponding class time, which you have been attending. If you need to switch, please let us know with at least one week's notice.

# Instructor Feedback Sessions

Our Week 5 workshop (the second-to-last session) will include optional time for work-in-progress presentations and feedback on your final project. Try to make sure you have at least a draft by then.

# Grading Rubric

| Criteria | Excellent (3) | Good (2) | Needs Improvement (1) |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| **Relevance** | Highly relevant to work/research; clear real-world value | Relevant; some real-world value | Not relevant or unclear value |
| **Integration of course themes** | Three or more themes, well connected into one solution | Two themes, at least loosely connected | Fewer than two themes |
| **Going beyond the course examples** | Two or more substantial extensions beyond the core course content | One extension, limited ambition | Direct copy of course examples |
| **Issues & mitigations** | Two or more relevant issues with concrete, realistic mitigations | Two issues, with generic or weak mitigations | Little or no discussion of issues |
| **Written document** | Clear, concise, complete; tools table and link included; under 50% AI on Pangram | Minor gaps or a missing element; or 50% AI or more on Pangram | Disorganized or missing several required elements |
| **Presentation & demo** | Clear, engaging presentation; compelling live demo | Clear presentation; demo with minor issues | Disorganized; no demo, or demo fails without backup |

# Frequently Asked Questions

## **How do I show that I used AI tools during the project?**

While lots of people are trying to prove they *didn't* use AI in their work, we actually want to see that you *did* use it (just not for writing your document)! This can be tricky to show, especially for things like data analysis where you could have done it all yourself. Here's how to handle this:

1.  **Keep track**: Take some screenshots or short videos of you working with AI tools, like keeping receipts to show what you did.

2.  **Show the difference**: Show how AI helped you do more than you could have done on your own. Kevin Scott, Chief Technology Officer at Microsoft, put it this way: "Work on problems that used to be impossible, but are now really hard." Build a project that you would not have been able to achieve (at least not within two weeks) without the help of AI tools.

## **Why must I write the document partly myself if this is an AI course?**

The document is where you show your own understanding: what you built, why, and what its limitations are. Use AI as much as you like for the solution itself.

## **Can I use AI tools not covered in the course?**

Yes! You're encouraged to explore additional AI tools. Just make sure at least two course themes are clearly represented.

## **What if my project doesn't work perfectly?**

That's completely fine and expected! Discuss what didn't work in your issues section and presentation. Failed experiments and limitations are valuable learning experiences.

## **Can I present preliminary results or a work-in-progress?**

It's okay if your work is not finished by the end of the course. Be clear about what's preliminary and what your next steps would be.

## **How strict is the 4-minute time limit?**

We'll aim for 4-5 minutes total to allow for brief Q&A. Practice your timing to ensure you cover all key points effectively.

## **Can I use the same data/project from another course?**

Yes, but you must add significant AI components that weren't part of your original work. The focus should be on the AI enhancement/integration.
